pages.title: Home
pages.content:
Q&A for people who ship software

Ask precise questions. Get answers that compile.

Devboard is a community forum for backend, frontend and infrastructure engineers. Post the stack trace, the query plan or the failing test, and get help from people who have debugged the same thing.

Browse questions
Create an account

1. Search first

Most questions have a cousin here already. Search the forums before posting.

2. Show your code

Paste a minimal example in a code block, with the exact error and versions.

3. Close the loop

Post what fixed it. Future you, and everyone else, will thank you.

pages.title: Posting Guidelines
pages.content:
Devboard is a place for specific, answerable technical questions and thoughtful discussion. Please read this before your first post.

Asking

  • Write a title that states the problem: “pgx: CopyFrom fails with numeric overflow”, not “Postgres issue”.
  • Include a minimal reproducible example in a code block, the exact error message and the versions involved.
  • Say what you already tried. It saves everyone a round trip.
  • Never paste secrets, tokens, customer data or production credentials. Redact them.

Answering

  • Explain why, not only what. Link to documentation where it helps.
  • Test your snippet or say clearly that you did not.
  • Disagree with the code, not the coder.

Moderation

Moderators may edit titles for clarity, close duplicates and remove spam. Promotional posts belong in Show & Tell, and only for things you built yourself.

Code of conduct

Harassment, discrimination and personal attacks are not tolerated. Report a post with the moderation tools or write to the moderators in Meta.

pages.title: About Devboard
pages.content:
Devboard is a small, independent Q&A community run by working engineers. It started as an internal help channel and opened to everyone when the questions got too good to keep private.

Why a forum?

Chat moves too fast and answers disappear. A forum keeps the question, the dead ends and the fix together, searchable for the next person who hits the same wall.

The stack

Devboard runs on Pursae with Pursae Forum: one Go binary and PostgreSQL. No JavaScript is needed to read, post or moderate.

topics.author: admin
topics.title: How to ask a good question on Devboard
topics.content:
Good questions get fast answers. Before you post:

  1. Search. Your question may already have an answer.
  2. Reduce the problem to the smallest piece of code that still fails.
  3. Paste it in a code block with the exact error and the versions you use.
  4. Say what you expected and what happened instead.

When an answer solves it, reply with what worked. See the posting guidelines for the rest.

replies.author: ana
replies.content: Adding one: never paste secrets. If you did, rotate them first and then ask a moderator to edit the post.

topics.author: dev
topics.title: Goroutine leak when the request context is cancelled
topics.content:
My worker pool keeps growing in production. runtime.NumGoroutine() climbs every time a client disconnects mid-request. The worker looks like this:

func worker(ctx context.Context, jobs <-chan Job) {
	for job := range jobs {
		process(job)
	}
}

The producer stops sending when the context is cancelled, but the workers never exit. What am I missing?

replies.author: kenji
replies.content:
Your workers block on range jobs forever because nobody closes the channel when the context ends. Select on ctx.Done() too:

func worker(ctx context.Context, jobs <-chan Job) {
	for {
		select {
		case <-ctx.Done():
			return
		case job, ok := <-jobs:
			if !ok {
				return
			}
			process(ctx, job)
		}
	}
}

And close jobs in the producer with defer close(jobs) so normal shutdown works as well.

replies.author: ana
replies.content: Add go.uber.org/goleak to your tests. It fails the test when goroutines are still running at the end, which catches this class of bug early.

replies.author: dev
replies.content: That fixed it. Goroutine count is flat now, and goleak found a second leak in a ticker I forgot to stop. Thanks both!

topics.author: kenji
topics.title: Postgres ignores my index for ILIKE '%term%'
topics.content:
This query does a sequential scan on 4M rows even though title has a B-tree index:

SELECT id, title FROM articles
WHERE title ILIKE '%' || $1 || '%'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows ~900 ms. Is there a way to make substring search use an index?

replies.author: ana
replies.content:
A B-tree can only help with a left-anchored pattern ('term%'). For substrings use a trigram index:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
CREATE INDEX articles_title_trgm ON articles USING gin (title gin_trgm_ops);

Trigram GIN indexes support LIKE and ILIKE with leading wildcards. Searches shorter than three characters still scan.

replies.author: lucia
replies.content: If you need ranking or stemming, look at full-text search with a tsvector column instead. Different tool, often a better fit for “search box” features.

replies.author: kenji
replies.content: Trigram index brought it down to 6 ms. Index build took 40 seconds with CONCURRENTLY. Marking this solved.

topics.author: sam
topics.title: Is :has() fast enough for a 5,000-row list?
topics.content:
I want to show a toolbar only when a row is selected, without JavaScript state:

.list:has(> .item.is-selected) .toolbar { display: flex; }

Does :has() cause noticeable style recalculation on large lists?

replies.author: lucia
replies.content: Anchoring it with the child combinator (>) like you did keeps invalidation cheap. Unanchored :has(.x) on a big subtree is where it hurts.

replies.author: sam
replies.content: Profiled in Chrome and Firefox: under 2 ms per selection change with 5,000 rows. Shipping it.

topics.author: lucia
topics.title: GitHub Actions cache misses on Go modules every run
topics.content: Every CI run downloads all modules again, although the cache step reports a save. Using a monorepo with go.mod in services/api.

replies.author: kenji
replies.content:
setup-go keys the cache on go.sum at the repository root by default. Point it at the real one:

- uses: actions/setup-go@v5
  with:
    go-version-file: services/api/go.mod
    cache-dependency-path: services/api/go.sum

replies.author: dev
replies.content: Same issue bit us. Also make sure you don't have a separate actions/cache step fighting over the same path.

topics.author: noor
topics.title: Refresh tokens: HttpOnly cookie or localStorage?
topics.content: We are redesigning auth for a single-page app with an API on the same site. Where should the refresh token live, and what do you do about CSRF if it's a cookie?

replies.author: sam
replies.content: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict (or Lax) cookie scoped to the refresh endpoint path. JavaScript never sees it, so XSS cannot steal it.

replies.author: ana
replies.content: With SameSite plus a custom header requirement on the refresh endpoint you get solid CSRF protection. Rotate the refresh token on every use and detect reuse.

replies.author: noor
replies.content: Going with the cookie, path-scoped, with rotation and reuse detection. Thanks for the sanity check.

topics.author: lucia
topics.title: Lifetimes in a struct that holds a &str
topics.content:
The compiler rejects this with expected named lifetime parameter:

struct Parser {
    input: &str,
    pos: usize,
}

I don't want to clone the input into a String. How do I express that the parser borrows it?

replies.author: kenji
replies.content:
Give the struct a lifetime parameter and tie the borrowed field to it. Tokens returned from the parser can then borrow from the input, not from the parser:

struct Parser<'a> {
    input: &'a str,
    pos: usize,
}

impl<'a> Parser<'a> {
    fn next_token(&mut self) -> Option<&'a str> { /* ... */ None }
}

replies.author: lucia
replies.content: Returning &'a str instead of &str was the missing piece. Compiles and no clones. Thanks!

topics.author: dev
topics.title: Moving a Flask service to Go: what did you miss most?
topics.content: We are porting a mid-sized Flask API to Go. For people who did this: what did you miss from Python, and what surprised you in a good way?

replies.author: kenji
replies.content: Missed: quick scripting and the REPL. Gained: one static binary, predictable memory, and a compiler that catches half of what our tests used to.

replies.author: sam
replies.content: Missed comprehension one-liners. Did not miss dependency resolution on deploy day.

replies.author: ana
replies.content: Keep the Python service running behind the same API contract and move one endpoint at a time. Contract tests saved us.

topics.author: kenji
topics.title: Show: a tiny terminal log viewer with level filters
topics.content:
I got tired of piping logs through three tools, so I wrote a small viewer that colours levels, follows files and understands JSON lines:

$ tail -f app.log | lumberjack --level warn --json
12:04:31 WARN  db    slow query 412ms  SELECT ... FROM orders
12:04:33 WARN  http  retrying POST /hooks/billing (attempt 2)

Single binary, no config. Feedback on the flags welcome.

replies.author: dev
replies.content: This is great. Could it read from journald directly?

replies.author: lucia
replies.content: Feature request: a --since 10m flag so I don't have to scroll back after an incident.

replies.author: noor
replies.content: Nice. Please make sure it never prints fields named password or token unmasked by default.
